opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think if you look at the big foundation model companies, the North Star is pretty clearly some version of general intelligence, and more concretely, a general-purpose assistant. The idea is that you build one model that's capable enough to help with almost any task you throw at it: writing code, drafting an email, answering a question, reasoning through a problem. A lot of the field's energy goes into making that assistant more capable, more reliable, and safer.

That's a really important direction, and I think it'll produce enormously useful tools. But it's also worth noticing what that framing optimizes for. The assistant paradigm is fundamentally about task completion. You have a goal, and the model helps you get there more efficiently. The metrics follow from that: benchmarks on coding, math, question answering.

What I find interesting, and where my own work sits a bit differently, is that these models have also learned something else from all the human data they're trained on. They've absorbed a lot about how people behave, how they talk, how they make decisions, how they relate to each other. That opens up a different kind of question. Instead of asking "how can this model do a task for me," you can ask "can this model help us simulate and understand human behavior?" That's the idea behind generative agents: using these models to create believable simulations of people and communities, which you could use to prototype social systems, test policies, or study social dynamics in ways that were previously really hard to do.

So I'd say the North Star for the big labs is the capable, general assistant. I think there's a complementary North Star that's just as exciting, which is using these models as a lens on ourselves, for modeling and understanding human behavior at scale.

r001.rationale: The response identifies general intelligence and a capable general-purpose assistant as the labs’ North Star, but does not say they aim to build superintelligent machines.

r002.rationale: It mentions coding, math, and question-answering benchmarks, but does not clearly state that the models are intended to excel at technical problems with objective answers.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the North Star for these companies has really been a search for general intelligence, and to be honest, I think they've gotten pretty far on it. The approach has been to scale up models and train them on everything, with the goal being a system that can do essentially any task a human can do, or at least any cognitive task.

But the thing I find interesting is that there's a distinction between being very intelligent and being very human. When you look at what these models are optimized for, it's correctness: being helpful, being accurate, being a good assistant. And that's a fantastic goal if what you want is a tool that gets things right. The model is, in a sense, trying to be the best possible version of an agent that answers your question.

What that doesn't naturally give you is a model of an actual person, with all the quirks, inconsistencies, and biases that real people have. If I ask a language model what it thinks about some policy, it's going to give me a thoughtful, balanced answer. If I ask a specific person in Ohio, they'll give me something very particular to their life, their history, their mood that day. And that specificity is exactly what you'd want if you're trying to simulate human behavior, whether that's for social science, for product testing, or for understanding how a community might respond to something.

So I'd say the North Star for the big labs is intelligence, and rightly so. The work I'm interested in sits a little bit to the side of that, asking: can we take these very capable models and use them to build believable proxies of actual humans, with their diversity intact, rather than one very smart generic agent?

r001.rationale: The response describes a goal of general intelligence and performing human cognitive tasks, but it does not identify building superintelligent machines as the goal.

r002.rationale: It says models are optimized for correctness and accuracy, but does not state that they are intended to excel at technical problems with objective answers.

astra-6.text: I think the North Star for these companies is artificial general intelligence—building systems that can perform a broad range of intellectual tasks at or beyond a human level. But I think there’s a complementary question that deserves attention: What kind of world do we want to build with that intelligence? Capability gives us more possibilities, but it doesn’t, by itself, tell us which possibilities are worth pursuing. For me, that means thinking about how these systems can help people understand one another, coordinate, and make better decisions.

r001.rationale: The response identifies AGI as the goal and describes systems performing a broad range of intellectual tasks at or beyond human level, which conveys building superintelligent machines.

r002.rationale: The response discusses broad capabilities and helping people, but does not say the models are intended to excel at technical problems with objective answers.

sol-6.1.text: I think the North Star for these companies is artificial general intelligence—building systems that can match or exceed human capabilities across a broad range of tasks. They may have different views on how to get there and how to do it safely, but that seems to be the shared ambition. What interests me is how that ambition connects to people: how we build AI that understands the social world and helps us navigate it.
